content: 1. Mohan R (2006) discussed preventive measures for leptospirosis, emphasizing the importance of rodent control as a key strategy to mitigate the risk of this bacterial infection. 2. Monahan AM, Miller IS, and Nally JE (2009) highlighted the risks of leptospirosis associated with recreational activities, particularly in water-based environments, and stressed the need for awareness and preventive measures. 3. Montalbano Di Filippo M et al. (2017) identified and analyzed the phylogenetic position of Naegleria species isolated from geothermal springs in Italy, providing insights into their ecological and potential pathogenic roles. 4. Morgan OW et al. (2010) reported on an outbreak of schistosomiasis among recreational users of the Upper Nile River in Uganda in 2007, underscoring the health risks associated with freshwater exposure in endemic regions. 5. Pagès F et al. (2016) investigated a leptospirosis outbreak among triathlon participants on Réunion Island in 2013, linking the infection to water exposure during the event. 6. Perkins A and Trimmier M (2017) reviewed recreational waterborne illnesses, focusing on their recognition, treatment, and prevention, with an emphasis on public health implications. 7. Phillips AE et al. (2018) presented baseline findings on urogenital schistosomiasis in Cabo Delgado, Mozambique, as part of the SCORE study, highlighting the disease's prevalence and impact in the region. 8. Picardeau M (2013) provided an overview of the diagnosis and epidemiology of leptospirosis, emphasizing the challenges in identifying and managing this zoonotic disease. 9. Pinto KC et al. (2012) assessed the microbiological quality of sand and water from three beaches in São Paulo, Brazil, identifying potential health risks from microbial contamination. 10. Plano LRW et al. (2011) studied the shedding of Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) by bathers in marine waters, highlighting the public health implications of these findings. 11. Roser DJ et al. (2015) developed dose-response algorithms for Pseudomonas aeruginosa folliculitis associated with waterborne exposure, providing a quantitative framework for risk assessment. 12. Röser D et al. (2018) examined schistosomiasis in Danish students after white-water rafting in Uganda, using serology and clinical findings to document the health risks of adventure tourism. 13. Rudko SP et al. (2018) utilized qPCR-based cercariometry to evaluate the risk of swimmer’s itch in recreational lakes, offering a novel approach to monitoring this parasitic condition. 14. Samba-Louaka A et al. (2019) explored the ecological and molecular characteristics of free-living amoebae and their associated microorganisms, shedding light on their potential health impacts. 15. Schets FM et al. (2011) investigated the presence of potentially pathogenic vibrios in marine and freshwater bathing waters, correlating their occurrence with environmental conditions and disease outcomes. 16. Schreiber PW et al. (2015) described a cluster of leptospirosis cases acquired through river surfing in Switzerland, emphasizing the need for preventive measures in recreational water activities. 17. Schwartz E et al. (2005) documented schistosome infections among river rafters on the Omo River in Ethiopia, highlighting the risks of waterborne parasitic diseases in endemic areas. 18. Sejvar J et al. (2003) reported leptospirosis cases among athletes participating in the Eco-Challenge in Malaysian Borneo in 2000, linking the outbreak to environmental exposure. 19. Selbach C et al. (2016) assessed the risk of swimmer’s itch in surface waters, using Lake Baldeney in Germany as a case study to evaluate the impact of environmental factors on disease prevalence. 20. Semenza JC et al. (2017) developed an early warning system for Vibrio infections in the context of a warming climate, demonstrating the influence of environmental changes on disease dynamics. 21. Shaw KS et al. (2015) evaluated recreational swimmers’ exposure to Vibrio vulnificus and Vibrio parahaemolyticus in the Chesapeake Bay, Maryland, USA, highlighting the public health risks of these pathogens. 22. Siddiqui R and Khan NA (2014) reviewed primary amoebic meningoencephalitis caused by Naegleria fowleri, discussing the challenges posed by this rare but fatal infection. 23. Soge OO et al. (2009) characterized methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species isolated from public marine beaches on the US West Coast, emphasizing their potential health risks. 24. Sokolow SH et al. (2016) conducted a global assessment of schistosomiasis control over the past century, demonstrating the effectiveness of targeting snail intermediate hosts in reducing disease transmission. 25. Soldánová M et al. (2013) reviewed the etiology, impact, and risk factors of swimmer’s itch in Europe, providing a comprehensive overview of this parasitic condition. 26. Sousa CA et al. (2012) reported on an ongoing outbreak of dengue type 1 in Madeira, Portugal, highlighting the public health response and epidemiological findings. 27. Sow S et al. (2011) examined the contribution of water contact behavior to high Schistosoma mansoni infection rates in the Senegal River Basin, emphasizing the role of human activity in disease transmission. 28. Stern EJ et al. (2010) described an outbreak of leptospirosis among adventure race participants in Florida in 2005, linking the cases to environmental exposure during the event. 29. Strathmann M et al. (2016) investigated the microbiological aspects of the River Ruhr in Germany, focusing on its use for recreation and as a raw water source for drinking water. 30. Sympardi S et al. (2019) presented a case of mucormycosis during a catastrophic flood in Mandra, Greece, in 2017, highlighting the health risks associated with extreme weather events. 31. Thapaliya D et al. (2017) studied the prevalence and characterization of Staphylococcus aureus and MRSA on public recreational beaches in Northeast Ohio, identifying potential health risks. 32. Tung MC et al. (2013) identified Naegleria fowleri from a hot spring in Taiwan, linking it to the first reported case of primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) in the country. 33. Vally H et al. (2004) reported an outbreak of Aeromonas hydrophila wound infections associated with mud football, emphasizing the risks of exposure to contaminated environments. 34. Vezzulli L et al. (2012) examined the long-term effects of ocean warming on prokaryotic communities, focusing on vibrios and their potential health implications. 35. Visvesvara GS et al. (2007) reviewed the pathogenic free-living amoebae Balamuthia mandrillaris, Naegleria fowleri, and Sappinia diploidea, discussing their clinical significance and challenges in management. 36. WHO (2006) provided guidelines for safe recreational water environments, focusing on swimming pools and similar settings to minimize health risks. 37. Zbikowska E et al. (2013) investigated the distribution of Legionella pneumophila and free-living amoebae in thermal saline baths used in balneotherapy, highlighting their potential health risks. 38. Zimmerman AB et al. (2016) discussed microbial keratitis associated with contact lens use, offering practical considerations for optometrists to prevent and manage this condition.
